newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Tokyo helps calm Euro markets early losses.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tokyo helps calm Euro markets early losses.

text.p: Soothing words from the Japanese government helped European financial markets recover from steep opening losses on Tuesday after Wall Street suffered its second largest points plunge ever.

European stocks were marked down across the board after the Dow Jones industrials tumbled 192 points, or 2.5 percent, on Monday. The sell-off was sparked by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's remarks about potential Japanese sales of U.S. government bonds.

The dollar also skidded more than one yen after Hashimoto, responding to a question after a speech in New York, said Japan had in the past been tempted to sell its holdings of U.S. Treasury securities and boost its gold reserves, but had not done so.

But European markets steadied after Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Tuesday that Hashimoto had been incorrectly reported. "The prime minister's real intention was not reported correctly," he said.

Large-scale Japanese purchases of U.S. bonds has helped underpin Wall Street's record-breaking bull run. A senior finance ministry official told reporters that American government bonds were an essential investment tool in Japan's foreign reserves.

The reassuring remarks seemed to calm volatile markets. The London stock market clawed back most of its opening losses of 0.8 percent and Paris rebounded into positive territory after starting down 0.5 percent. The dollar climbed back close to Monday's levels after falling overnight to 114.10 yen.

Even before Japan's damage limitation exercise, London's early losses were milder than the Dow's dive. The blue-chip FTSE index's recent weak performance, which has seen it retreat 4.5 percent from its June 13 closing high, limited the severity of Tuesday's markdown.

"London's been pulling back six days on the trot," one dealer said. "It's more important to look at the Wall Street fall in percentage terms, which is not so dramatic. We're not going to just shrug our shoulders and ignore it, but that should put us in a calmer frame of mind."
Any sign that the Wall Street plunge was not a one-off correction could spell more pain for the FTSE, dealers said.
"Hitherto every fallback on Wall Street has been regarded as a buying opportunity," one said. "But one or two people are getting slightly sceptical."

The FTSE's six-day losing streak was provoked by concern about higher interest rates and the new Labour government's July 2 budget, which may abolish tax breaks on dividend payments for big institutional investors like pension funds.
French stocks climbed 0.5 percent after the Japanese finance ministry's remarks, which helped wipe out opening index losses.

State-controlled French bank Credit Lyonnais was among the biggest early gainers with a 4.50 percent jump after a newspaper report that it expected a two billion franc ($343.7 million) profit for 1997 after a cost-cutting programme.

Frankfurt recovered from a weak opening after Wall Street to show only modest losses by mid-morning. The dollar's recovery helped but volumes remained thin with little corporate news to give direction.

In currency markets, the dollar rebounded to 114.84 yen by mid-morning from overnight lows of 114.10 when Hashimoto's remarks sent markets reeling. It was at 115.31 yen in late Europe trade on Monday.

"Markets were hit quite badly. We will now see a period characterised by denial and rebuttal from Japan. And by the time the U.S. opens this afternoon there should be a renewed calm and stability," said Julian Fisher, economist at Daiwa Europe.
"I wouldn't be surprised if we saw some bounce-back both in the dollar and in the treasury markets."

Analysts said Hashimoto's comments reflected Japan's frustration at American warnings that Japan should not let its trade surplus balloon again. U.S. President Bill Clinton warned Japan on Sunday that it risks an economic war with the U.S. if the surplus explodes again.
CURRENCIES AT 1000 GMT
The dollar was at 1.7235 marks and 114.84 yen, compared with 1.7210 and 115.31 in late European trade on Monday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1000 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 1.6 points at 4,574.2.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was up 18.37 points at 2,780.45.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was down 1.46 at 3753.26.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was at $339. 45 in early trade, against $338.90 at the close on Monday. Silver was at $4.83, up four cents. ($ = 5.818 French Francs)
